title: A small repo's git history told as a story: what each commit changed and why
summary: Eleven commits from a fictional plant-tracker repo, read as decisions instead of diffs - a history is a story about what the author was worried about.

blocks.title: A log is a story if you read the why
blocks.body: This fictional repo tracks one backyard greenhouse: a sensor, a spreadsheet habit, and eleven commits over five months. Read as diffs it is dull. Read as decisions, it is the story of what its author kept worrying about - in order.

items.title: init: temperature logger that prints to the console
items.detail: The smallest thing that could possibly work. One sensor, one number, zero structure. Every repo starts as a dare.

items.title: add: write readings to a CSV with timestamps
items.detail: The first worry: memory. Printing was not enough; the author wanted to look back. Note what is not here yet - no tests, no config.

items.title: fix: handle the sensor returning nothing
items.detail: The first scar. Something failed in the real world and the code admits it now. Null readings get skipped, logged, and counted.

items.title: add: daily summary row - min, max, mean
items.detail: The second worry: meaning. A pile of readings is not an answer. The repo starts summarizing instead of just collecting.

items.title: refactor: split logging from summarizing
items.detail: Two jobs were living in one file. No behavior changed; the shape of the code admitted what it had become.

items.title: add: humidity sensor
items.detail: Scope grows, and the June refactor is what made it cheap. Histories are full of these quiet payoffs.

items.title: fix: CSV columns drifted when humidity was missing
items.detail: A real bug with a real lesson: the file format was a promise, and July 4 had quietly broken it. The fix adds a header row and pins column order.

items.title: add: tests for the CSV writer
items.detail: Tests arrive late - after the first format bug, not before. That is how most test suites are actually born: as a memorial to a specific failure.

items.title: add: alert if temperature drops below 4 C overnight
items.detail: The third worry: being told. The repo stops waiting to be read and starts speaking up. A watcher script, an email, done.

items.title: fix: alert fired three times for one cold night
items.detail: Alert fatigue gets its own commit. One night, one alert; the code learns to latch until conditions clear.

items.title: docs: README with wiring photo and setup steps
items.detail: The final commit here is for the next person - who is the author, in March, having forgotten everything. Documentation is a letter to your future self.

blocks.heading: The shape underneath
blocks.body: Three worries, in order: remember (May), understand (June), be told (August). Each worry arrived only after the previous one was solved, and each fix commit taught something the feature commits could not. That is a normal, healthy history: needs appear in sequence, and the code grows a layer per need instead of guessing all of them on day one.

blocks.heading: What the fix commits were really saying
rows: Real hardware fails; plan for it
A file format is a promise; version it or pin it
An alert is a contract with the reader's attention
blocks.caption: Fix commits are the most honest lines in any history.

blocks.heading: Reading any history this way
items: Read the commit messages newest-to-oldest once, then oldest-to-newest - the story only runs one direction.
Mark each commit as feature, fix, refactor, or docs. The ratio tells you the era the repo is in.
Ask of each fix: what assumption died here? That is the author's real education.
Ask of each gap: what was happening in the six quiet weeks? Sometimes the answer is the code just worked.

blocks.heading: Check the story
blocks.prompt: The tests arrived on August 2, months after the first feature. What does that timing usually mean?
options: A specific failure taught the author what to test
The author was careless until August
The repo was not real code until it had tests
blocks.explanation: Late-arriving tests usually memorialize a bug - here, the July 19 CSV drift. Healthy histories show tests born from specific failures, not from abstract guilt.
